toc.title: Your body is compelled to regulate
How trauma gets in the way
One thing you can do now

blocks.p: In the journey of trauma recovery, understanding self-regulation and building trust in your body's natural capacity for healing is important, though difficult. I'm going to make the case that your body is compelled to self-regulate, and that trauma stops this natural process. Then I'll describe how you can get unstuck by allowing your natural capacity for self-regulation to happen, and give you a starting point for what you can do now.

Trauma is the inability to access our polyvagal state of safety and social engagement. It's being stuck in a defensive state, or being easily triggered into a defensive state, and not being able to self-regulate out of it.
So trauma is not just what you went through. Trauma is the impact of what you went through, or of what you didn't go through, like having healthy attachment when you were growing up.
Therapists use all kinds of modalities to help their clients recover from trauma. I have my own approach, the Polyvagal Trauma Relief System, and it has three very specific phases:

ol: Learn the science. Learn the Polyvagal Theory and other foundational pieces. This normalizes what you're going through and builds a new narrative for the self, which can reduce self-judgment, blame, and shame.
Increase and maintain access to your safety state. This increases your distress tolerance, which prepares you for phase three.
Directly unstuck. Go after the stuck defensive state, through it and with curiosity, and self-regulate mindfully through it by actually attuning to the dysregulation.

blocks.p: This piece is mostly phase one. It also touches on phase two, and it ever so lightly grazes phase three: allowing the stuck defensive state to be present.

blocks.h: Your body is compelled to regulate

blocks.p: Regulation is a biological compulsion. Our bodies are compelled to regulate. They must regulate.

Do you remember learning about homeostasis in grade school? Encyclopedia Britannica says that homeostasis is "any self-regulating process by which biological systems tend to maintain stability while adjusting to conditions that are optimal for survival. If homeostasis is successful, life continues. If unsuccessful, disaster or death ensues."

So homeostasis, self-regulation: pretty darn important. Regulation optimizes our cells, our biology, our self-maintenance, and it increases our potential for successful reproduction. On a biological level, it's very important to self-regulate. And as mammals, we are the most self-regulated when we have access to our polyvagal state of safety and social engagement. Those pathways are where we can optimize health, growth, and restoration.

Porges, through the Polyvagal Institute, says the Polyvagal Theory links our biological imperative to connect with others to neural pathways that calm our autonomic nervous system. In the context of mammalian physiology, these systems are foundational processes through which behavioral experiences can lead to sociality and optimal health, growth, and restoration.
So self-regulation is something we must have.

blocks.h: How trauma gets in the way

blocks.p: Trauma disrupts the natural process of self-regulation. When you're traumatized, you're stuck in a defensive state, with less access to your polyvagal safety state and your potential for connection. You're stuck in flight, fight, shutdown, or freeze.

If you don't have access to your safety state, numerous potential health problems result. The adverse childhood experiences study showed this. One of the things it found was that as the number of adverse childhood experiences, or ACEs, increases, so does the risk for negative outcomes. Those outcomes are not just psychological and behavioral, but physical too.

So the more traumatic experiences someone has, the more negative effects they live with, across all areas of life, not just psychologically. That's because the body is unable to regulate itself and access its safety state, and optimal homeostatic functioning is lost.

To recover from trauma, then, you need to return to self-regulation and allow it. That's the umbrella answer. If you can do that, your autonomic nervous system will shift out of its stuck defensive state and more and more into its polyvagal state of safety.

The next step is to understand what's preventing self-regulation, because I don't think you're doing it on purpose. None of us stays stuck in a defensive state on purpose. If we could simply choose to be unstuck, I'm sure you'd do it right now.

A whole bunch of things get in the way of self-regulation, but I group them into two: you keep yourself stuck, and we keep each other stuck. Here I'll focus briefly on how you keep yourself stuck, and I break that into two kinds of adaptations.

A behavioral adaptation is a behavior you engage in as an adaptation to your stuck defensive energy. It's something you do to reduce the discomfort or pain you're going through. It reduces the intensity of your stuck defensive state, but it also stops you from climbing the [polyvagal ladder](piece:autonomic-nervous-system): coming up out of shutdown into fight, up from fight into flight, or releasing stuck freeze energy.

Behavioral adaptations can be so many things: substance use, self-harm, disordered eating, bullying. It could be mindless phone swiping. Anything we do to reduce the intensity of what we're going through.

The other way you keep yourself stuck is through cognitive adaptations. These are top-down skills you use to cope with the pain of your stuck defensive state. They're basically the same as behavioral adaptations, except that rather than an actual behavior, they're a thought-based thing.
I should be clear that Dr. Porges did not differentiate between cognitive and behavioral adaptations. That's my own insertion into the theory, not warranted or sanctioned or asked for.
There are a whole bunch of cognitive adaptations that distract us or reduce the intensity of what we're going through:
All of these focus us on the outside world or keep us stuck in our thoughts, rather than letting us attune to what's happening within, from the bottom up.

These behavioral and cognitive adaptations are things you might be doing to reduce your defensive activation. You're probably not doing them on purpose. It's more of a habit or a reflex. And in a way, they've worked. They may have reduced your emotional dysregulation. They may have thwarted a panic attack or two or three or four. Maybe they got your mind off something painful.

So they've worked, in a way. But it might be time to try something different. I think mindfulness, and actually experiencing what you have inside, might be where you need to go. Maybe not right now, and maybe not directly into the stuck pain, but eventually, I think this is where we need to end up.

So hear me out. To self-regulate out of a stuck traumatized state, you must first be able to allow the defensive activation and actually feel your feelings. A lot of good can be done by simply focusing on your polyvagal safety state. But to truly get unstuck, to take that next step in trauma recovery, I think you eventually need to be able to mindfully feel your feelings.

That takes mindfulness: the ability to exist in the present moment with curiosity. You anchor yourself in your polyvagal safety state, exist in the present moment, and then bring that anchored safety to your stuck defensive state.

Once you're firmly anchored in safety, you can exist in the present moment, and you can be curious. Being in the present moment connects your cognitive processes with your bottom-up experiences. It aligns your thoughts with what's happening within you, and calms them enough to focus on the bottom-up experience. As the interference from your thoughts diminishes, and your behavioral adaptations diminish too in that moment, you actually align with what's happening within you. Then self-regulation can potentially unfold naturally.

This might sound scary. Maybe it's terrifying you. I know. It requires a lot of trust in your natural capacity to self-regulate. I started by saying that you must self-regulate. Now I'm saying you have to trust your capacity to do it.

Your response might be, "I can't," and you might be right. If you tried this right now, in this moment, it might be too much to ask. But as you work on your safety state, eventually you may be able to, and at that point it will take some trust.

Self-regulation is not a conscious choice. It's a biological mechanism that requires trust in the present moment: trusting that you're able to self-regulate, that your body is able to heal or recover, however you want to say it, to get unstuck.

We can create situations where self-regulation is more likely. We can pick the right environment, set the right mood, be with safe people, practice breathing skills. But trust is also needed, trust in yourself and in what your body can do.

When your stuck defensive state emerges and tries to unstuck itself, it might be overwhelming, especially if you're not prepared for it. So part of this is trust, and part of it is preparing yourself by building the strength of your safety state. As your state tries to discharge or climb the polyvagal ladder, difficult emotions, memories, sensations, and impulses will probably emerge. If you have freeze energy within you, you're going to feel the fear of your freeze immobility, and maybe not just fear, but overwhelm, panic, or even rage.
Even in the face of these difficult emotions, trust is necessary. You need to trust that your body can navigate them, and that you can allow them, witness them, and experience them.

It won't just be emotions. There will be sensations and impulses underneath the emotions that come up as well. If you can mindfully experience your emotions, that opens an avenue for self-regulation to unfold. And as your body goes through that natural self-regulation, sensations and impulses will emerge from it.

As you feel an impulse, you need to act on it: mindfully allow it, and act on it. If there's an impulse to slowly emerge from shutdown, maybe by very slowly reorienting to the environment, you allow it and mindfully experience it. From your fight state, you might feel an impulse to squeeze. Can you allow that and mindfully experience it in a very safe, non-destructive way, like with a fidget?

I love rubber hedgehog rings. They're more like bracelets, rubber, with spikes all over them, and they're really good for squeezing, pulling, and twisting. When I get more of that aggressive fight energy in my system, I like to pull them a lot. I just pull, and I feel my chest, my back, and my shoulders, those muscles flexing. It's phenomenal.

If these impulses come up and you're not able to act on them, it's probably not time for you to mindfully allow your defensive activation. You'd probably benefit more from building the strength of your safety state.

All of these connect: state, sensation, impulse, emotion, and cognition. They all connect through your polyvagal state. Eventually, you want to allow that stuck defensive state to exist in the present moment, consciously and with curiosity, and to welcome it and experience it in all of those pieces: the state, the sensations, the impulses, the emotions, and the cognitions that come along with it.
That might be a terrifying idea, but I think we can make it manageable. Here's the broad view of how to allow defensive activation:

ol: Anchor in safety first. That's really the key. The safety state is vital for self-regulation to happen effectively.
Observe with curiosity. Anchored in safety, you'll have the curiosity to observe your stuck defensive state without judgment.

blocks.p: Anchoring in safety and then allowing defense once is not enough. It's something to return to continually. It's a long process, and it won't be done all at once. Think of it like working out a muscle and building its strength. Same thing with the safety state.

Traumatized people have a compromised safety state. Those safety pathways aren't strong enough yet, or access to them is easily lost when there's a certain trigger in the environment. For all of us, but maybe for traumatized people in particular, it's really important to keep exercising access to your safety state first.

Then, eventually, after anchoring in safety, you allow some defense, just a little bit, like dipping a toe in the water, and come back to safety. Think of it like a safety sandwich: you start in safety, touch into defense ever so lightly, and come back to safety.

It's really important to build tolerance for defensive activation during trauma recovery, because it's going to come up. Practicing being in your safety state builds your capacity to access it and exist in it.

blocks.why: This article talks about anchoring in safety. This practice does just that, tuned to you.

blocks.p: I know this might sound scary, but welcoming your defensive activation is not only okay, it's necessary in the trauma recovery process eventually. If you simply focused on building the strength of your safety state, I think you could have a much more meaningful, functional, and fulfilling life. But if you want to take that next step and truly recover from trauma, the next step is to mindfully allow that defensive activation, or what's left of it, because I don't think it'll be nearly as dysregulated by then.
We don't address the defensive activation all by itself, and we don't address it all at once. We go at it while anchored in safety.

When you're anchored in safety, you should eventually feel curiosity or interest. I call this the safety state's interest impulse. When you feel that interest, "What the heck is going on inside of me? What is this like?", that's a sign you're ready to begin self-regulation.

Then you remain anchored in your safety state while you allow defense. The purpose is to allow defense and self-regulation, but maintaining access to your safety state is the priority. If you lose access and spiral into a dysregulated state, there probably won't be much benefit to the attempt at all.

blocks.h: One thing you can do now

blocks.p: Here's one thing you can do right now, or as soon as possible, to aid your trauma recovery.
Check your immediate environment, at work or at home or wherever you are, and ask yourself how you feel there:

ul: Do you feel more safe or less safe?
Do you feel more like you can breathe, or less?
Do you feel more like smiling, or less?

blocks.p: Then alter one thing in the environment now to increase the passive safety cues entering your system. Pick one thing you can change: open the blinds, open a window and let in fresh air, clean up clutter, tidy your space, or remove knick-knacks that aren't benefiting you.
This little thing doesn't heal your trauma. I know that. But it does provide more safety cues and passively remind your body that you're safe. These are passive things that are neurocepted as safety.

That's just for right now. Do more when you can, and not just in your environment. What about the music you listen to? What alterations can you make there? The movements you do? The things you spend your time doing? Do a little audit. Take your own inventory. What can you alter to give yourself more safety?
Increase your safety experiences. That builds the strength of your safety state, and you know by now how important that is.
